questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has chronic gout with many tophi on his hands and elbows. His serum urate stayed high despite allopurinol and then febuxostat. He now receives an intravenous infusion of a PEGylated recombinant enzyme every 2 weeks. The day after his first infusion he has fatigue, dark urine and yellow eyes. Laboratory results: hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL (it was 14.0 g/dL a week ago), indirect bilirubin 3.8 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase markedly high and haptoglobin undetectable. A blood smear shows bite cells, and a later test shows glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. Which molecule, made by the reaction this drug catalyzes, most likely caused his red cell injury?
questions.explanation: **Pegloticase** is a recombinant **uricase** that oxidizes uric acid; the reaction makes **hydrogen peroxide** and, at the end, **allantoin**. Red cells with **G6PD deficiency** cannot make enough NADPH to keep glutathione reduced, so the peroxide oxidizes hemoglobin and causes **hemolysis** (and sometimes methemoglobinemia). Allantoin is the main end product, but it is harmless and very water-soluble; that is why uricase lowers urate so well. Oxypurinol (the active metabolite of allopurinol) and peroxynitrite are not products of uricase.
questions.explanation_pt: A **pegloticase** é uma **uricase** recombinante que oxida o ácido úrico; a reação produz **peróxido de hidrogênio** e, no final, **alantoína**. As hemácias com **deficiência de G6PD** não produzem NADPH suficiente para manter a glutationa reduzida, então o peróxido oxida a hemoglobina e causa **hemólise** (e às vezes metemoglobinemia). A alantoína é o principal produto final, mas é inofensiva e muito hidrossolúvel; por isso a uricase reduz tão bem o urato. O oxipurinol (metabólito ativo do alopurinol) e o peroxinitrito não são produtos da uricase.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man has had four gout attacks in the past year. His kidney function is normal. He starts a new oral drug to lower serum urate. Three weeks later he has severe left flank pain and passes a small stone that does not show on a plain abdominal x-ray. His laboratory results before and after the new drug are: serum urate 9.4 mg/dL before and 6.1 mg/dL after; 24-hour urinary uric acid 520 mg/day before and 960 mg/day after. Which mechanism best explains the effect of this drug?
choices: Inhibition of xanthine oxidase in the liver
Enzymatic breakdown of uric acid to allantoin
Binding to tubulin, which blocks neutrophil migration into joints
Blockade of urate reabsorption in the proximal tubule
questions.explanation: Serum urate fell while **urinary uric acid almost doubled**, so the drug works by making the kidney excrete more urate. **Uricosuric drugs** such as **probenecid** block **URAT1**-mediated urate reabsorption in the proximal tubule, and the high urate load in the urine can form radiolucent **uric acid stones**. A xanthine oxidase inhibitor also lowers serum urate, but it makes less uric acid, so urinary uric acid would fall, not rise. A uricase drug would also lower urinary uric acid, and colchicine does not change urate levels.
questions.explanation_pt: O urato sérico caiu enquanto o **ácido úrico urinário quase dobrou**, então o fármaco age fazendo o rim excretar mais urato. Os **uricosúricos**, como a **probenecida**, bloqueiam a reabsorção de urato mediada pelo **URAT1** no túbulo proximal, e a grande carga de urato na urina pode formar **cálculos de ácido úrico** radiotransparentes. Um inibidor da xantina oxidase também reduz o urato sérico, mas diminui a produção de ácido úrico, então o ácido úrico urinário cairia, e não subiria. Um fármaco com uricase também reduziria o ácido úrico urinário, e a colchicina não altera os níveis de urato.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old woman has severe nodular acne with scarring that did not improve with topical drugs and an oral antibiotic. She starts an oral vitamin A derivative. She uses two forms of contraception and has a monthly pregnancy test. Three months later she has very dry, cracked lips and dry eyes. Her fasting laboratory results at baseline and now are: triglycerides 115 mg/dL and 1,180 mg/dL; total cholesterol 170 mg/dL and 245 mg/dL; ALT 22 U/L and 41 U/L (reference 7-35 U/L). Which acute complication is she at greatest risk for because of these laboratory changes?
questions.explanation: **Isotretinoin** often raises serum lipids, and a very high **triglyceride** level is a well-known cause of **acute pancreatitis**. The drug is usually stopped or the dose lowered when triglycerides rise this much. Isotretinoin can also cause **idiopathic intracranial hypertension** (especially with tetracyclines), but that is not caused by her lipid or liver results. The small rise in ALT is common and mild; it does not suggest that acute liver failure is coming.
questions.explanation_pt: A **isotretinoína** muitas vezes eleva os lipídios séricos, e um nível muito alto de **triglicerídeos** é uma causa bem conhecida de **pancreatite aguda**. Em geral, o fármaco é suspenso ou a dose é reduzida quando os triglicerídeos sobem tanto. A isotretinoína também pode causar **hipertensão intracraniana idiopática** (sobretudo com tetraciclinas), mas ela não decorre dos resultados lipídicos ou hepáticos. A pequena elevação da ALT é comum e leve; não sugere insuficiência hepática aguda iminente.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis takes tizanidine for leg spasticity. Two days ago she started ciprofloxacin for a urinary tract infection. Today she is very drowsy and feels faint when she stands up. Blood pressure is 84/50 mm Hg, pulse is 46/min and respirations are 14/min. Her pupils are small but react to light. Ciprofloxacin inhibits the liver enzyme that normally clears tizanidine. What is the mechanism of action of tizanidine?
choices: Agonism at GABA-B receptors in the spinal cord
Blockade of the ryanodine receptor in muscle
Enhancement of GABA-A chloride channel opening
Blockade of nicotinic receptors at the end plate
questions.explanation: **Tizanidine** is a **central α2-adrenergic agonist**, similar to clonidine. It reduces spinal motor neuron excitation, and at high levels it lowers sympathetic outflow, which causes **hypotension**, **bradycardia** and sedation. **Ciprofloxacin** inhibits **CYP1A2**, which metabolizes tizanidine, so drug levels rise sharply. **Baclofen** is the tempting choice because it also treats spasticity and causes drowsiness, but it is a GABA-B agonist and does not typically cause this clonidine-like picture.
questions.explanation_pt: A **tizanidina** é um **agonista α2-adrenérgico central**, semelhante à clonidina. Ela reduz a excitação dos motoneurônios espinais e, em níveis altos, diminui o tônus simpático, causando **hipotensão**, **bradicardia** e sedação. O **ciprofloxacino** inibe a **CYP1A2**, que metaboliza a tizanidina, então os níveis do fármaco sobem muito. O **baclofeno** é a escolha tentadora porque também trata a espasticidade e causa sonolência, mas é agonista GABA-B e não costuma causar esse quadro semelhante ao da clonidina.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman has rheumatoid arthritis that is still active on weekly methotrexate. Her physician adds an oral small-molecule drug that she takes twice a day. It blunts the intracellular signals of several cytokine receptors, including those for IL-6 and interferons. Four months later she has burning pain and then clusters of vesicles in a band on the left side of her chest that stops at the midline. Which mechanism of the added drug best explains this complication?
questions.explanation: This is **herpes zoster**, the classic infection linked to **JAK inhibitors** such as **tofacitinib**. Cytokine receptors (IL-6, interferons and others) signal through **Janus kinases** and STAT proteins; blocking them weakens antiviral immunity, so latent varicella-zoster virus can reactivate. **Leflunomide** is the most tempting option because it is also an oral DMARD added to methotrexate, but it blocks pyrimidine synthesis and does not act on cytokine receptor signals. Abatacept blocks B7-CD28 costimulation, but it is an injected fusion protein, not an oral small molecule.
questions.explanation_pt: Trata-se de **herpes-zóster**, a infecção clássica associada aos **inibidores de JAK**, como o **tofacitinibe**. Os receptores de citocinas (IL-6, interferons e outros) sinalizam por meio das **Janus quinases** e das proteínas STAT; bloqueá-las enfraquece a imunidade antiviral, e o vírus varicela-zóster latente pode se reativar. A **leflunomida** é a opção mais tentadora porque também é um MMCD oral associado ao metotrexato, mas ela bloqueia a síntese de pirimidinas e não age na sinalização dos receptores de citocinas. O abatacepte bloqueia a coestimulação B7-CD28, mas é uma proteína de fusão injetável, e não uma molécula pequena oral.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has severe plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis. He starts a monoclonal antibody that he injects under the skin, and his skin clears well. Five months later he has white plaques on his tongue that scrape off and leave a red base. He also has 6 weeks of bloody diarrhea and crampy abdominal pain. Colonoscopy shows patchy ulcers with normal mucosa between them, and biopsy shows noncaseating granulomas. Which molecule is the most likely target of his antibody?
choices: The p40 subunit of IL-12 and IL-23
questions.explanation: **Secukinumab** blocks **IL-17A**, which recruits neutrophils and keeps mucosal barriers strong against **Candida**, so **mucocutaneous candidiasis** is a typical adverse effect. IL-17 blockade can also **cause or worsen inflammatory bowel disease**, here Crohn disease. **Ustekinumab** is the most tempting choice because it also acts on the Th17 pathway (through IL-23), but it is used to **treat** Crohn disease rather than trigger it. TNF-α inhibitors are also effective treatments for Crohn disease.
questions.explanation_pt: O **secuquinumabe** bloqueia a **IL-17A**, que recruta neutrófilos e mantém as barreiras mucosas fortes contra a **Candida**, então a **candidíase mucocutânea** é um efeito adverso típico. O bloqueio da IL-17 também pode **causar ou piorar a doença inflamatória intestinal**, aqui a doença de Crohn. O **ustequinumabe** é a escolha mais tentadora porque também age na via Th17 (por meio da IL-23), mas é usado para **tratar** a doença de Crohn, e não a desencadeia. Os inibidores de TNF-α também são tratamentos eficazes para a doença de Crohn.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy has atopic dermatitis on his eyelids and face. For a year his parents applied a potent topical glucocorticoid to these areas almost every day. The skin there is now thin and shiny, with visible small blood vessels. His physician stops the glucocorticoid and prescribes tacrolimus ointment, which does not cause skin atrophy. What is the mechanism of action of tacrolimus?
choices: It binds FKBP12, and the complex inhibits mTOR
It binds cyclophilin, and the complex inhibits calcineurin
It activates a cytoplasmic receptor that represses inflammatory genes
It binds FKBP12, and the complex inhibits calcineurin
It inhibits phosphodiesterase 4 in inflammatory cells
questions.explanation: **Tacrolimus** binds **FKBP12**, and the complex inhibits **calcineurin**. Without calcineurin, the transcription factor **NFAT** stays phosphorylated in the cytoplasm, so T cells make less **IL-2** and other cytokines. Unlike glucocorticoids, it does not reduce collagen synthesis, so it does not cause **skin atrophy** or telangiectasia; this makes it useful on the face and eyelids. **Sirolimus** also binds FKBP12, but that complex inhibits **mTOR**, not calcineurin; cyclophilin is the binding protein of cyclosporine.
questions.explanation_pt: O **tacrolimo** se liga à **FKBP12**, e o complexo inibe a **calcineurina**. Sem a calcineurina, o fator de transcrição **NFAT** permanece fosforilado no citoplasma, e os linfócitos T produzem menos **IL-2** e outras citocinas. Ao contrário dos glicocorticoides, ele não reduz a síntese de colágeno, então não causa **atrofia cutânea** nem telangiectasias; por isso é útil na face e nas pálpebras. O **sirolimo** também se liga à FKBP12, mas esse complexo inibe o **mTOR**, e não a calcineurina; a ciclofilina é a proteína de ligação da ciclosporina.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman has had rheumatoid arthritis for 5 years, and it is well controlled on leflunomide. She now wants to become pregnant. Her physician stops leflunomide and explains that the active metabolite can stay in the blood for many months. To speed its removal, he gives oral cholestyramine until two blood tests show that the drug level is very low. How does cholestyramine shorten the time that the drug stays in the body?
choices: It binds the drug in the gut and blocks its recycling
It induces the liver enzymes that metabolize the drug
It increases the secretion of the drug by the renal tubules
It displaces the drug from albumin so it can be filtered
It acidifies the urine and traps the drug in ionized form
questions.explanation: The active metabolite of **leflunomide** (teriflunomide) is strongly protein-bound and undergoes **enterohepatic recirculation**: it is excreted in bile and then reabsorbed from the gut. **Cholestyramine**, a bile acid-binding resin that is not absorbed, **binds the drug in the intestine** so it leaves in the stool, which cuts its long half-life. This matters because leflunomide is **teratogenic**. Cholestyramine does not induce liver enzymes; enzyme inducers such as rifampin work in a different way and are not used for this washout.
questions.explanation_pt: O metabólito ativo da **leflunomida** (teriflunomida) liga-se fortemente às proteínas e sofre **recirculação entero-hepática**: é excretado na bile e depois reabsorvido no intestino. A **colestiramina**, uma resina sequestradora de ácidos biliares que não é absorvida, **liga-se ao fármaco no intestino** para que ele saia nas fezes, o que encurta sua meia-vida longa. Isso importa porque a leflunomida é **teratogênica**. A colestiramina não induz enzimas hepáticas; indutores enzimáticos como a rifampicina agem de outra forma e não são usados para essa eliminação.
